name: effectivity
intent: Attach an explicit validity period - a Range of dates - to a fact or relationship, so every reader can ask "is this true on date D?" and get a defined answer instead of inferring history from insertion and modification timestamps.
problem: Some facts hold only for a while: an employment, a price, a tariff, a regulation, an address, a role assignment, a permission. Without a validity period the model can only answer "what is in the database now": historical questions are unanswerable, future-dated changes need a job that edits rows on the day, and a late correction silently rewrites what was previously believed.
context: Domain models and stores where individual facts have a bounded lifetime and the as-of date is part of the question - pricing and tariffs, employment and contracts, regulatory or tax rules, organisational assignments, access grants, subscriptions. The pattern applies when only part of the data (not every attribute of an object) needs history, and when the domain itself understands that the fact has a period.
benefits: The validity question gets one owner: the period answers "when", the record answers "what", instead of every caller guessing from timestamps.
Future and historical facts are modelled uniformly - a period starting next month is stored today and read like any other, with no scheduled job that mutates rows at midnight.
As-of queries stay simple and indexable: one predicate on the range (or one range containment operator) instead of application-side filtering over a full history.
Corrections are expressible: a retroactive change replaces the period explicitly, so the previous timeline is a recorded decision rather than an overwritten accident.
The same structure works in memory and in the store - a Range value plus a date predicate maps directly onto two date columns or a native range type, so the domain and the schema stay aligned.
History is preserved by construction: a new period is a new row/instance, which makes audit and reproducibility questions answerable without a separate logging scheme.
tradeoffs: Clients must be temporal-aware: every read that wants "the fact as of now" has to add the effectivity predicate, so the pattern buys an explicit query cost that a plain record does not pay.

A missing period is indistinguishable from a false fact unless the model says otherwise - a query that finds nothing may mean "not effective then", "not yet recorded" or "data gap", and returning null hides the difference.

Overlapping periods make the as-of answer ambiguous, so either a constraint must reject them (unique/exclusion constraint, aggregate invariant) or a precedence rule must be written down and tested; leaving it implicit means the database decides by accident.

Retroactive corrections need a primitive interface (set the range directly) beside the convenience operations; an in-place correction that is not modelled explicitly destroys the evidence of what was believed before.

Boundary semantics are a permanent source of off-by-one bugs: closed versus half-open end, sentinel end dates such as 9999-12-31, date-only boundaries stored as instants, and zones that make a period end in the middle of its last day.

Read and storage cost: a range predicate and index on every query, range joins instead of equality joins for many-to-many validity, and one row per change so history grows with every price or assignment change.
Bi-temporal tracking (valid time plus transaction time) is a second range and hands the double predicate back to every caller - the complexity the pattern tried to hide returns at the query surface.

participants.responsibility: The domain fact or relationship that is true only for a while (employment, price, membership, assignment), modelled as its own record so that a new period is a new instance rather than an edit of an existing one.

Value object holding the validity period with explicit bound semantics (inclusive start, exclusive end or an explicitly closed pair) and an open end for "until further notice"; it owns containment and overlap operations.
Every read that must respect time passes an explicit as-of date and filters with the range instead of reading the current clock implicitly inside domain logic.
Decides and enforces what concurrent and adjacent periods mean for one identity: non-overlap rejected at write time, or a documented precedence order; it also decides what a gap means.
The primitive operations that correct the timeline (set the range directly) beside the convenience operations (start on a date, end on a date) that cover the ordinary additive case.

use_cases: Employment and contract periods: one person holds two employments during a handover month, each with its own validity range, and "which company employed X on date D" is a containment query rather than a guess.

Price lists, tariffs and rate cards: an article has a sequence of prices, the price valid on the invoice date is the one that must be billed, and a price change is entered weeks before it takes effect.
Regulatory and tax rules: a threshold, rate or obligation is valid from a legislative date and replaced later, so a calculation for a historical period must use the rule set that was effective then.

Organisational and role assignments: who managed which unit, which cost centre belonged to which division, which supplier supplied which part with which share - effective-dated so reorganisations do not erase the previous structure.
Access grants and entitlements: a role, licence, subscription or territory grant is effective for a period, so "was this allowed at that moment" remains answerable after the grant is revoked.
Insurance, warranty and subscription terms: cover, excesses and renewal terms change on effective dates, and claims or invoices must be judged against the terms in force at the event date.

Contract and price validity in commerce and procurement: price lists, discount condition records, purchase agreements and carrier tariffs are valid only for a period, so an order, receipt, shipment or invoice must be priced against the agreement in force for the reference date, not the newest one on file (Oracle SCM pricing; SAP MM condition records; freight tariff resolution).

Manufacturing engineering changes: a BOM line, routing or revision is in effect from a date or serial number onward; production orders and field service resolve the structure effective at the order date or unit number, with overlap and gap rejected at change-draft time (SAP ECM parameter effectivity; PeopleSoft BOM revision maintenance).

Insurance cover and health-plan benefits: policy endorsements split the term, benefit versions and coverage spans decide what is payable for a loss date, a service date or a prescription, and retroactive changes force reprocessing or recalculation of closed periods (Salesforce endorsement versioning; Guidewire PolicyPeriod; Oracle HI policy versions; 834/271 eligibility).

Effective-dated rates, fees and market data in banking and asset management: interest rates, margins, promotional offers and reference prices carry an effective date and remain applicable until superseded, with back-dated corrections recalculating accruals and already-liquidated cycles (Oracle lending interest/fee modules; LUSID/IVP reference data).

HR master data as a platform primitive: Workday separates the effective date (when a change to a business object goes into effect - past, present, or future) from the entry date (when the change was actually recorded), so as-of reports over hires, salary changes and eligibility are a first-class capability rather than an application-layer convention; PeopleSoft makes the same structure a platform convention with EFFDT as a key field plus EFF_STATUS and EFFSEQ to disambiguate same-date rows; ServiceNow capacity and crew assignments carry Effective from/Effective to with validation rules that reject ranges conflicting with existing usage (Workday Administrator Guide; PeopleTools Application Designer; ServiceNow FSM documentation).
avoid_when: A creation or modification timestamp answers the real question ("when was this row written"): an audit column is enough and a validity range only adds a predicate to every read.
Most attributes change over time, or the domain refers to versions such as contract amendments: use Temporal Object (or a system-versioned table) instead of a range per record.
The facts are immutable events ("the price changed on 3 March"): store the events and derive periods, rather than keeping an effectivity range that duplicates event order.

The platform already maintains history - SQL:2011 system-versioned tables, PostgreSQL application-time tables with WITHOUT OVERLAPS, an event store with as-of projections: do not hand-roll a second timeline beside it.
No historical or future-dated question has ever been asked: a range plus an index plus a temporal predicate is real cost for a capability nobody uses.
The period would only ever be "since creation until deletion" and deletion already exists: the row lifecycle is the effectivity, and a second representation can only disagree with it.
anti_patterns: Overlapping periods for the same identity with no precedence rule: the as-of query answers differently depending on row order or index choice.
A sentinel end date (9999-12-31, 12/31/9999) used for "open": it leaks into durations, ages, exports and reports and silently becomes a real date.
A nullable end date that means both "still effective" and "end unknown", so the two cases cannot be told apart in queries or analytics.
Storing an instant (timestamp with time zone) for the end of a date-granularity period, so the fact ends in the middle of its last day for some zones and stays valid past it for others.
A denormalised is_current flag next to the range, maintained by a different code path; after the first missed update the flag and the dates disagree and no reader knows which one is authoritative.
Retroactive correction by editing the existing range in place, destroying the previous timeline and any evidence that the fact was once believed differently.
Re-deriving effectivity from created_at/updated_at columns: the answer changes whenever a row is touched for an unrelated reason.

Mixing closed [start, end] and half-open [start, end) conventions in the same codebase — the freight industry calls this 'the root of most resolution defects' — so different queries or services give contradictory answers for the same as-of date.

A nullable end date that means both 'still effective' and 'end unknown', so the two cases cannot be told apart in queries or analytics, and a future decision to close the period silently changes historical interpretation.

Using a maximum-date sentinel (9999-12-31, 12/31/9999) for open periods: it leaks into duration arithmetic, ages, exports and reports, and silently becomes a real date when a far-future event is recorded.
Overlapping periods for the same identity with no precedence rule: the as-of query returns whichever record the plan reaches first — enforced by a database accident rather than by design.
design_principles: Separate the validity question from the fact: one place answers "when" (the range), the record answers "what".
Model the period as a value object with explicit bound semantics instead of passing two loose dates through every signature.
Make the as-of date an explicit input to the query; never let the current time be ambient inside domain or repository logic.
Single owner for the non-overlap (or precedence) invariant: enforce it where periods are written, not where they are read.
History is immutable in effect: corrections extend or explicitly reset ranges, they do not silently rewrite what a reader saw before.
Keep the mapping between the in-memory range and the stored representation trivial (half-open pair, closed pair, native range type) so no conversion hides a boundary shift.
best_practices: Adopt one bound convention - half-open [from, until) with an open end for "until further notice" - and use it identically in memory, in the store and in the API.
Use a date-only type for date-granularity facts (LocalDate, DateOnly, PlainDate, civil::Date) and reserve instants for period boundaries that genuinely happen at a time of day.

Enforce non-overlap where the data is written: an exclusion/unique constraint for the stored form, an aggregate invariant for the in-memory model, or a written-down precedence rule where overlaps are intended (salary versus bonus).
Offer both interfaces: convenience operations (startOn(date), endOn(date)) for the common additive case and a primitive setEffectivity(range) used only for retroactive corrections.
Make the as-of parameter mandatory in the query API and inject the current date in exactly one place (the application service or the job), never in the repository.
Test the boundaries explicitly: the start date, the day before it, the end date, the day after, an empty period and a date inside a known gap.
Index the range (or the two date columns) and keep a separate index for the current period when "current" is the hot query.
Decide what a gap means and encode it in the result type (no record versus not effective) instead of returning null from a finder.
When a correction changes history that other facts referenced, record the correction as its own action so downstream recomputation is possible.

Detect and name gaps explicitly: when a date falls between two closed periods with no overlap, encode the result type so callers can distinguish a gap from "not yet recorded" rather than returning null and conflating all three cases.

Store the open end as NULL (or an explicit 'open' marker), never as a sentinel date — a sentinel leaks into duration arithmetic, exports and age calculations and silently becomes a real date; Oracle's Temporal Validity demonstrates that NULL is the correct representation of "until further notice".

Coalesce adjacent periods when values are identical: when one period ends and the next begins with the same attribute values, merge them into a single continuous period to keep the table well-formed and prevent spurious gaps from appearing in as-of queries.

Keep period boundaries as date-only types (LocalDate, DateOnly, civil::Date) for business facts that operate on calendar days; use timestamp-with-timezone only when the fact genuinely occurs at a time of day, and apply the timezone once at the boundary, not to every row.

Test the full boundary matrix explicitly: the start date, the day before it, the end date, the day after, an empty period, a date inside a known gap, a date inside an overlapping pair, and the open-end sentinel — these eight cases catch most off-by-one errors.

When adding effectivity to existing data for the first time, decide what "unknown start" means (NULL, epoch, or domain minimum) and document it; back-filling a start date from a creation timestamp is a heuristic, not a fact, and should be marked accordingly.

When a retroactive correction touches other facts that referenced the old period, record the correction as its own action (a domain event or an audit entry) so downstream recomputation is triggered and the correction is not silently absorbed.

For high-update entities (prices, exchange rates), consider a materialized current-state view or a filtered index on the open period so the hot path ("what is current") does not pay the full temporal join cost on every query.

Document the bound convention in the schema itself: add a named CHECK constraint like check_validfrom_before_validto or a comment on the range column so the half-open [from, until) semantics is unambiguous to every future reader.
sources: Richard T. Snodgrass and Ilsoo Ahn, "Temporal Databases", IEEE Computer 19(9), September 1986 — establishes the valid-time / transaction-time taxonomy and the four database classes (snapshot, rollback, historical, temporal); the canonical origin of the vocabulary the effectivity pattern reuses. https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.1986.1663327

C. E. Jensen, C. E. Dyreson et al., "A Consensus Glossary of Temporal Database Concepts", SIGMOD Record 23(1), March 1994 (revised in LNCS 1399, Springer 1998) — authoritative glossary: valid time = when a fact is true in reality; transaction time = when the fact is stored; lifespan; period; bitemporal interval. https://www2.cs.arizona.edu/~rts/pubs/SIGMODRecordMarch94p52.pdf

Christian S. Jensen and Richard T. Snodgrass, "Semantics of Time-Varying Information", Information Systems 21(4), 1996 — deep treatment of the valid/transaction time model, events-versus-states duality, and temporal dependency theory; the formal underpinning of the pattern's tradeoffs. https://www2.cs.arizona.edu/people/rts/pubs/ISJune96.pdf

Richard T. Snodgrass, Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL, Morgan Kaufmann 2000, Ch. 2 — defines valid-time state tables via FROM DATE/TO DATE columns; states the two-pass design method and the constraint/complexity cost of adding temporal attributes. https://www2.cs.arizona.edu/~rts/tdbbook.pdf

Krishna Kulkarni and Jan-Eike Michels, "Temporal features in SQL:2011", ACM SIGMOD Record 41(3), September 2012 — normative description of PERIOD FOR, closed-open periods, WITHOUT OVERLAPS temporal primary keys, FOR PORTION OF DML, and the three table modes (application-time, system-versioned, bitemporal). https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/1209/pdfs/07.industry.kulkarni.pdf

James F. Allen, "Maintaining Knowledge about Temporal Intervals", Communications of the ACM 26(11), November 1983 — defines the 13 mutually-exclusive interval relations (before, meets, overlaps, during, starts, finishes and inverses) and the transitivity table; the formal basis of every period predicate. https://doi.org/10.1145/182.358434

Michael H. Boehlen, Richard T. Snodgrass and Michael D. Soo, "Coalescing in Temporal Databases", VLDB 1996 — defines when adjacent or overlapping value-equivalent periods may be merged; proves which operators preserve or destroy coalescing; evidence for the one-row-per-change storage cost. https://www.vldb.org/conf/1996/P180.PDF

Martin Fowler, "Effectivity" (eaaDev draft, 7 March 2004) — add a time period to an object to show when it is effective; additive versus retroactive updates; recommends Range over date pairs. https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/Effectivity.html

Martin Fowler, "Bitemporal History", April 2021 — actual/record dimensions, append-only record history over mutable actual history, sally.salaryAt(actualDate, recordDate), when bi-temporal is avoidable and why it significantly complicates systems. https://martinfowler.com/articles/bitemporal-history.html

Andy Carlson, Sharon Estepp and Martin Fowler, "Temporal Patterns", PLoP'98 — Temporal Property, Temporal Association, Snapshot; states Time Period as an application of Range; Temporal Association described as a use of Effectivity. https://www.hillside.net/plop/plop98/final_submissions/P09.pdf

Massimo Arnoldi, Kent Beck, Markus Bieri and Manfred Lange, "Time Travel: A Pattern Language for Values That Change", EuroPLoP 1999 — Version History, Perspective, Effective Date, Period Enumeration, Long Transactions; separates posting date from effective date as two dimensions of time. https://hillside.net/europlop/HillsideEurope/Papers/EuroPLoP1999/1999_LangeEtAl_TimeTravel.pdf

Vlad Khononov, Learning Domain-Driven Design, O'Reilly 2021, Ch. 7 "Modeling the Dimension of Time" — the DDD answer to temporal modeling: event-sourced domain model as the primary tool, with temporal patterns as the non-ES alternative. https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/learning-domain-driven-design/9781098100124/

Mathias Verraes, "Temporal Modelling", GOTO 2019 — models events and processes as first-class building blocks; passage of time as a domain event; frames temporal analysis as a domain-analysis technique for DDD. https://verraes.net/2019/06/talk-temporal-modelling/

NILUS, "Temporal Modeling in Event-Driven Systems", June 2025 — every event should carry event time / recorded time / effective time; corrections are new events, never silent updates; bounded contexts own local timelines. https://www.nilus.be/blog/temporal_modeling_in_event-driven_systems/

Microsoft Learn, "Temporal Tables" (SQL Server 2016+) — system-versioned tables with PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME, GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START/END, FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF; SQL Server supports transaction time only; T181 application-time period tables are unsupported per MS-TSQLISO02. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/tables/temporal-tables

Oracle VLDBG, "Using Temporal Validity" (12c+) — PERIOD FOR user-defined valid-time dimension; AS OF PERIOD FOR and VERSIONS PERIOD FOR queries; NULL end = open-ended without sentinel; combined with Flashback Data Archive for bitemporal. https://docs.oracle.com/database/121/VLDBG/GUID-AF78C832-516A-4686-9DDF-CE12597F7723.htm

Paul A. Jungwirth, "Survey of SQL:2011 Temporal Features", 2019 — cross-vendor survey: DB2 (fullest: all three modes + temporal PKs), SQL Server (system time only), Oracle (app-time + own transaction time), PostgreSQL (extension only). https://www.illuminatedcomputing.com/posts/2019/08/sql2011-survey/

freightbill.org, "Contract Versioning & Effective Dating" — freight audit engine schema: closed-open [start, end) ranges, tstzrange column, EXCLUDE constraint for non-overlap; never-UPDATE amendment protocol; gap and non-determinism failure modes named. https://www.freightbill.org/freight-contract-architecture-rate-mapping/contract-versioning-effective-dating/

Oracle Fusion Cloud SCM, "Manage Pricing's Effectivity Dates" — pricing entities carry start/end dates; PriceAsOf and PricingDate drive price determination; price commitment business driver. https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/supply-chain-and-manufacturing/26b/faupr/manage-your-effectivity-dates.html

SAP MM, "Price Condition Records" — Valid From/Valid To on condition records; governance rule prohibits blank Valid To as it causes stale prices to be applied after renegotiation. https://sap.gugulii.com/docs/s4-mm/mm-a06-04/

HL7 FHIR R5, Coverage.period — "a missing end date means the coverage is continuing to be in force"; Condition.onset/abatement model valid time separately from recordedDate (transaction time). https://www.hl7.org/fhir/R5/coverage-definitions.html

Salesforce Insurance, "Policy Endorsements and Versioning" — endorsement splits the policy term: original version ends one day before endorsement effective date; endorsed version becomes active; together represent the complete policy across time. https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ind.ins_brokerage_billing_policy_endorsements_and_versioning.htm

XTDB, "Time in Finance" tutorial — eight named requirements: audit & replay, snapshot-free reporting, interleaving upstream sources, corrections via FOR PORTION OF VALID_TIME, scheduled effectivity, what-if scenarios. https://docs.xtdb.com/tutorials/financial-usecase/time-in-finance.html

LUSID (Finbourne), "What is bitemporal data?" — effectiveAt (valid time) vs asAt (transaction time); perpetual vs time-variant entity classification; instrument events are effective-dated. https://support.lusid.com/v1/docs/what-is-bitemporal-data

ISO 10303-41 (STEP), effectivity_schema — product-data definition: dated_effectivity (possibly open-ended interval), serial_numbered_effectivity, lot_effectivity, time_interval_based_effectivity; the formal ISO counterpart to the application-level Effectivity pattern. https://ap238.org/SMRL_v8_final/data/resource_docs/fundamentals_of_product_description_and_support/sys/12_schema.htm

ISO/TS 10303-1059 (Effectivity Application) — Effectivity_assignment with roles actual/planned/required; Ineffectivity_assignment (assigned items are not effective); Effectivity_relationship with constraint/inheritance relation types. https://ap238.org/SMRL_v8_final/data/modules/effectivity_application/sys/4_info_reqs.htm

PostgreSQL 19 documentation, 5.7 Temporal Tables — application time as a start/end period, WITHOUT OVERLAPS temporal primary keys, temporal foreign keys requiring the referenced row to exist throughout the referencing period. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/19/ddl-temporal-tables.html

Boris Novikov, "PostgreSQL Temporal Tables: Saving Data", Redgate Simple Talk, 2024 — EXCLUDE USING GIST as the temporal replacement for UNIQUE, and temporal DELETE as closing the period rather than removing the row. https://www.red-gate.com/simple-talk/databases/postgresql/making-temporal-databases-work-part-3-saving-data/

The Art of PostgreSQL, "Range Types and Temporal Constraints" — tstzrange/tstzmultirange with overlap (&&) and containment (@>) operators and a GiST exclusion constraint for non-overlapping periods. https://theartofpostgresql.com/yesql/data-schema-design/range-types/

Workday Administrator Guide, "Concept: Effective and Entry Dates" — effective date = when a change goes into effect (past/present/future), entry date = when it was recorded; reports can be bound by either; both are stored in the processing user's time zone, which shifts as-of results. https://doc.workday.com/admin-guide/en-us/reporting-and-analytics/custom-reports-and-analytics/set-up-reports/dan1370796621462.html

Oracle PeopleTools, "Effective Dates" (Application Designer Developer Guide) — EFFDT as a key field maintaining history/current/future rows, EFF_STATUS A/I for correct row selection, EFFSEQ to order multiple rows sharing one effective date; guidance to use EFFDT only on records that genuinely maintain history. https://docs.oracle.com/en/applications/peoplesoft/peopletools/8.63/application-designer-developer-s-guide/effective-dates.html

Zhiyue Yi, "Design a Table to Keep Historical Changes in Database", DEV Community — critique of EffectiveFrom/EffectiveTo as a history mechanism: versioning a row with a new surrogate id churns identity, breaks child-table joins, and complicates integrity; history/audit tables recommended when the real requirement is change tracking, not valid time. https://dev.to/zhiyueyi/design-a-table-to-keep-historical-changes-in-database-10fn

Michelle Feltman, "Just How Many Dates Do You Want? The Multiple Personality of Time in Your Data Warehouse", SAS SGF 29 — open (effective-from-until-superseded) versus closed (from/to) periods, when dual dates are genuinely required (insurance) versus when a single start date suffices, and the anti-pattern of overusing single-date records where dual dates are needed. https://support.sas.com/resources/papers/proceedings/proceedings/sugi29/110-29.pdf
